source_text: Hunc igitur agnoscimus et scimus deum, conditorem rerum omnium, dominum, propter potestatem, et parentem propter institutionem: hunc inquam, qui dzx7t, et facta sunt omnia; praecepit, et processerunt uniuersa; de quo scriptum est: omnia in sapientia fecisti; de quo Moyses: deus in caelo sursum et in terra deorsum; qui secundum Isaiam mensus est caelum palmo, terram pugillo: qui aspicit terram, et facit eam tremere: qui continet gyrum terrae, et eos qui habitant in ipso quasi locustae: qui expendit montes in pondere, et nemora in statera, id est certo diuinae dispositionis examine: ac, ne facile in ruinam procumberet magnitudo inaequaliter iacens, si non paribus fuisset librata ponderibus, onus hoc moderanter terrenae molis aequauit. qui dicit per prophetam: ego deus, et non est praeter me. qui per eundem prophetam refert quoniam matestatem meam non dabo alter’; ut omnes cum suis figmentis ethnicos excludat et haereticos, probans deum non esse qui manu artificis factus sit, nec eum qui ingenio haeretici fictus sit. non est enim deus, cui, ut sit, quaerendus est artifex. adhuc adiecit per prophetam: caelum mihi thronus est, terra autem scabellum pedum meorum: qualem mihi aedificabitis domum, aut quis locus requiei meae? ut ostendat quoniam multo magis illum templum non capit, quem mundus non capit. et haec non ad sui iactantiam, sed ad nostri scientiam refert. neque enim ipse a nobis desiderat magnitudinis gloriam, sed nobis uult religiosam, qua pater, conferre sapientiam. quique praeterea ferinos nostros animos et de agresti immanitate tumidos et abruptos ad lenitatem trahere uolens, dicit: ef super quem requiescet spiritus meus, nisi super humilem et quietum, et trementem uerba mea? ut deum aliquatenus quantus sit possit agnoscere, dum illum per spiritum collatum discit timere. qui similiter adhuc magis in notitiam nostri uolens peruenire, ad culturam sui nostros excitans animos, aiebat: ego sum dominus, qui feci lucem et creaui tenebras; ut uicissitudinum istarum quibus noctes diesque moderantur non naturam nescio quam putaremus artificem, sed deum agnosceremus potius (quod erat uerius) conditorem. quem quoniam obtutu oculorum uidere non possumus, de operum magnitudine et uirtute et maiestate condiscimus: uisibilia enim ipsius, inquit apostolus Paulus, a creatura mundi per ea quae facta sunt intellecta conspiciuntur; sempiterna quoque eius uirtus et diuinitas: ut animus humanus ex manifestis occulta condiscens, de operum magnitudine, quae uideret, mentis oculis artificis magnitudinem cogitaret. de quo idem apostolus: reg? autem saeculorum immortali, inuisibili, soli deo honor et gloria, euasit enim oculorum contemplationem, qui cogitationis uicit magnitudinem: guoniam, inquit, ex ipso et per ipsum et in ipso sunt omnia, nam et imperio eius omnia, ut ex ipso sint: et uerbo eius digesta, ut per ipsum sint: et in iudicium eius recidunt uniuersa, ut dum ” ipso exspectant libertatem corruptione deposita, in ipsum uideantur esse reuocata.
pass_a_gloss: We recognize and know this God, the creator of all things, the Lord, because of His power, and the Father because of His institution. This is the One who spoke and all things were made; He commanded and all things came into being. It is written of Him: You made all things in wisdom. Moses also says of Him: God is in heaven above and on earth below. According to Isaiah, He measured the heaven with a span and the earth with a fist. He looks at the earth and makes it tremble. He holds the circle of the earth and those who inhabit it like locusts. He weighs the mountains in a balance and the forests in a scale, that is, with a certain examination of divine disposition. And so that the greatness of the earth would not easily fall into ruin because it was unevenly laid out, if it had not been balanced with equal weights, He moderated this burden of earthly mass. He says through the prophet: I am God, and there is no one besides Me. He also says through the same prophet that He will not give His glory to another, in order to exclude all gentiles with their figments and heretics, proving that God is not one who was made by the hand of an artisan, nor one who was invented by the mind of a heretic. For He is not God if an artisan is needed to make Him exist. He added through the prophet: The heaven is My throne, and the earth is the footstool of My feet. What kind of house will you build for Me, or what place will be My rest? This shows that the temple cannot contain Him, just as the world cannot contain Him. And He says this not to boast about Himself, but to give us knowledge. For He does not desire glory from us, but wants to give us religious wisdom, as a Father. And because He wants to draw our wild minds, which are swollen and rough from their rustic savagery, to gentleness, He says: On whom will My Spirit rest, if not on the humble and quiet and those who tremble at My words? So that we may know how great God is, while we learn to fear Him through the Spirit that is given. He also says, wanting to come to our knowledge and stirring our minds to worship Him: I am the Lord, who made light and created darkness, so that we would not think that some nature is the artisan of these alternations by which nights and days are moderated, but rather that we would recognize God as the Creator, which is true. Since we cannot see Him with our eyes, we learn from the greatness and power and majesty of His works. For the apostle Paul says: The invisible things of Him are perceived and understood from the creation of the world through the things that were made; also, His eternal power and divinity. So that the human mind, learning from manifest things, may think about the magnitude of the Creator from the greatness of the works that it sees. The same apostle says: Now to the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, the only God, be honor and glory. He has escaped the contemplation of the eyes, who has overcome the magnitude of thought. For it is said: For from Him and through Him and in Him are all things, for all things are from His command, so that they may be from Him. And all things are arranged by His word, so that they may be through Him. And all things return to His judgment, so that, while they await freedom from corruption, they may be seen to be returned to Him.

pass_b_english: We recognize and know this God as the Creator of all things: the Lord because of His power, the Father because of His institution. He is the One who spoke, and all things were made; He commanded, and all things came into being. Of Him it is written: 'You made all things in wisdom' (Psalm 104:24). Moses also says of Him: 'God is in heaven above and on earth below' (Deuteronomy 4:39). According to Isaiah, He measured the heavens with a span and the earth with a fist (Isaiah 40:12). He looks at the earth and makes it tremble. He holds the circle of the earth and its inhabitants like locusts. He weighs the mountains in a balance and the forests in a scale—that is, by a certain examination of divine disposition. And so the greatness of the earth would not easily fall into ruin, since it was unevenly laid out, He moderated this burden of earthly mass by balancing it with equal weights.

He says through the prophet: 'I am God, and there is no one besides Me.' He also says through the same prophet that He will not give His glory to another (Isaiah 42:8; 48:11), in order to exclude all gentiles with their figments and heretics, proving that God is not one made by the hand of an artisan, nor one invented by the mind of a heretic. For He is not God if an artisan is needed to make Him exist. He added through the prophet: 'Heaven is My throne, and earth is the footstool of My feet. What kind of house will you build for Me, or what place will be My rest?' (Isaiah 66:1–2). This shows that the temple cannot contain Him, just as the world cannot contain Him. And He says this not to boast about Himself, but to give us knowledge. For He does not desire glory from us, but wants to give us religious wisdom, as a Father.

And because He wants to draw our wild minds—swollen and rough from rustic savagery—to gentleness, He says: 'On whom will My Spirit rest, if not on the humble and quiet and those who tremble at My words?' (Isaiah 66:2). So that we may know how great God is, while we learn to fear Him through the Spirit that is given. He also says, wanting to come to our knowledge and stirring our minds to worship Him: 'I am the Lord, who made light and created darkness' (Isaiah 45:7), so that we would not think some nature is the artisan of these alternations by which nights and days are moderated, but rather that we would recognize God as the Creator, which is true.

Since we cannot see Him with our eyes, we learn from the greatness and power and majesty of His works. For the apostle Paul says: 'The invisible things of Him are perceived and understood from the creation of the world through the things that were made; also His eternal power and divinity' (Romans 1:20). So that the human mind, learning from manifest things, may think about the magnitude of the Creator from the greatness of the works that it sees. The same apostle says: 'Now to the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, the only God, be honor and glory' (1 Timothy 1:17). He has escaped the contemplation of the eyes, who has overcome the magnitude of thought. For it is said: 'For from Him and through Him and in Him are all things' (Romans 11:36), for all things are from His command, so that they may be from Him. And all things are arranged by His word, so that they may be through Him. And all things return to His judgment, so that, while they await freedom from corruption, they may be seen to be returned to Him.
